newsitem.title: USA: Fraud case smacks of Venezuelan revenge, lawyer says.
newsitem.headline: Fraud case smacks of Venezuelan revenge, lawyer says.

text.p: The lawyer for a Cuban-born banker accused of bank fraud said Thursday that Orlando Castro Llanes was set up by the Venezuelan government, which was seeking revenge.

"Venezuela considers him to be a political enemy," lawyer Richard Sharpstein said in opening statements to the jury in Manhattan Supreme Court. He said the case against Castro Llanes should not be prosecuted in New York.

Castro Llanes, his son Orlando Castro and grandson Jorge Castro Barredo are accused of illegally using deposits in a family controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR), to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
Lead prosecutor Richard Preiss said the evidence will show that the transactions occurred in Manhattan and that all three defendants were part of the scheme to defraud.
"They recorded their thefts as assets," Preiss said.

The complicated financial case is being tried in New York because prosecutors claim money in the alleged fraud was transferred through New York banks, including two multimillion dollar transfers. The issue of jurisdiction will eventually be decided by the jury.

For more than 90 minutes the prosecutor went into detail describing the case and urging jurors to use their "common sense" in finding the three men guilty. More than one juror nodded off during his lengthy presentation.

Sharpstein accused the Manhattan District Attorney's office of "doing the bidding for the Venezuelan government." He said Castro Llanes was "set up" by the Venezuelan government until he was forced to flee the country in 1994.

The prosecutor said the three bankers misled Venezuelan depositors to believe BPIPR was a safe off-shore bank subject to tight regulatory control, attracting deposits of more than $55 million. Preiss said BPIPR closed down in January 1995 with uninsured losses to depositors of more than $15 million.
According to Sharpstein, Castro built a small empire in Venezuela that included 40 radio stations, four insurance firms, car rental companies and coffee manufacturing plants.
"He is an innovator. He is a Vanderbilt, a Rockefeller, a Ted Turner," the lawyer said. "He earned his money the old- fashioned way. This man came from nothing to become a millionaire."
Lawyers for the other two defendants will give opening statements Friday.
